explanations.explanation: Four days, baker. John 11:17 says Lazarus had already spent four days in the tomb when Jesus arrived. That's the number the text gives. I think this is a heavy part of the story, so I'll let that number sit.

Two is a number you'll find in this chapter, but not here. After Jesus heard the news, He stayed where He was two more days (John 11:6). The text says Lazarus had already spent four days in the tomb when Jesus arrived. So the count is four, and I can see how the two slipped in.

Seven shows up in a lot of places, so I get the reach. But John 11:17 gives a different number: four days in the tomb. Nothing in this passage mentions seven. Stick with what the text counts, friend, and the story gets clearer.
Not quite, friend. Martha went out to meet Him, but Mary stayed at home. The two sisters were in different places at that moment. Mary doesn't come out until Martha calls her aside (John 11:28).
That's right. Martha heard Jesus was coming and went out to meet Him, but Mary stayed at home. Only one sister goes out at that point. Mary gets there a little later, once Martha calls her aside.

explanations.answer: God will give Jesus whatever He asks
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's what she says: “But even now I know that God will give You whatever You ask of Him.” Look at those two words after “But,” "even now." Her brother has been in the tomb four days, and she still says it to Jesus's face. I think that's some real nerve.

explanations.answer: Lazarus is resting at peace with God
explanations.explanation: Martha never says that. What she says she knows is that God will give Jesus whatever He asks of Him. She's talking about Jesus and what God does for Him. Nothing in her words is about how Lazarus is doing right now.

explanations.answer: Jesus came as fast as He could
explanations.explanation: Martha doesn't say a word about how fast Jesus traveled. She says her brother would not have died if Jesus had been there. Then she says what she knows: God will give Him whatever He asks. The text leaves out how fast He came, so I'll leave it out too.

explanations.answer: In the resurrection at the last day
explanations.explanation: Yes! Martha says, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day.” She's got her answer ready, like a baker who already knows the recipe. She's pointing to the last day. Jesus is about to say something that changes how she hears it.

explanations.answer: Three days after he was buried
explanations.explanation: Martha doesn't give a count of days. She says he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day. Lazarus is already four days in the tomb, so a three-day timeline wouldn't fit anyway. Her eyes are on the last day.

explanations.answer: Once the time of mourning is over
explanations.explanation: Martha doesn't mention mourning ending at all. She points to the resurrection at the last day. It's a statement about what she knows, not about when her sadness will lift. The text gives her the last day, so that's the answer.
True! Jesus says, “Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies.” Even though he dies, friend. Jesus isn't skipping past death. He's saying what happens to the one who believes in Him.

Jesus does say it. His words to Martha are, “Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies.” So it isn't false, it's right there in the text. He says it straight to a woman standing in the middle of her grief.

explanations.answer: That He is the Christ the Son of God
explanations.explanation: That's it! Martha answers, “Yes, Lord,” and then says, “I believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God, who was to come into the world.” Notice she says it right after He asked, plain and sure. She doesn't have the whole story yet, but she knows who she's talking to.

explanations.answer: That He is a great prophet from Galilee
explanations.explanation: Martha says something bigger than that. She tells Him, “I believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God, who was to come into the world.” Nothing in her answer mentions a prophet or Galilee. She names Him as the Christ and the Son of God.

explanations.answer: That He is the prophet Elijah returned
explanations.explanation: Elijah was an Old Testament prophet (1 Kings 17:1), but Martha doesn't mention him. She says she believes Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, who was to come into the world. That's the whole confession. The text has her calling Jesus "Lord" first and then saying exactly who she believes He is.
Yes, quickly! John 11:29 says Mary "…got up quickly and went to Him." She doesn't wait around. Martha says one sentence and Mary is already out of her seat.
The text says the opposite. Mary got up quickly and went to Him. In fact the Jews in the house noticed how quickly she got up (John 11:31). Nobody could miss it.

The text doesn't describe Mary that way. It says she got up quickly and went to Him. The word is about how fast she moved, and the Jews in the house saw it too. I'd have been out the door faster than a cookie sheet leaving the oven.
Yes. The text says they followed her, “…supposing she was going to the tomb to mourn there.” They were guessing, and as it turns out, the guess didn't match where she went. Mary went to Jesus.

The text doesn't give that as their guess. It says they supposed she was going to the tomb to mourn there. The temple isn't mentioned anywhere in these verses. They saw how quickly she got up, and they followed her with the tomb in mind (John 11:31).

Jerusalem is mentioned in this passage, since Bethany was a little less than two miles away. But that's not where the Jews thought Mary was headed. They supposed she was going to the tomb to mourn there. That's their guess, and it was about the tomb.

True! Martha said, “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.” Mary comes, falls at His feet, and says, “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.” Same sentence, word for word. I think those words must have meant a lot to both of them.

Look again, friend. Martha says, “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.” Mary says exactly that when she reaches Jesus. The two sisters said the same words, each when she met Him (John 11:21, 32).
Yes. Jesus asks, “Where have you put him?” It's a short question, and they answer, “Come and see, Lord…” That's all He asks in that moment.
Jesus doesn't ask that. The question in the text is, “Where have you put him?” He asks where Lazarus is, and they answer, “Come and see, Lord…” Nothing about the sickness comes up here.

explanations.answer: Who was with him at the end
explanations.explanation: That question isn't in the text. Jesus asks, “Where have you put him?” and they say, “Come and see, Lord…” It's a question about a place. The text doesn't have Him ask about who was there.
That's right. The Jews said, “See how He loved him!” They watched Jesus weep and that's what they saw. It's the first thing they say about it.

explanations.answer: See how He grieves for the sisters
explanations.explanation: That's not what they say. The text says, “See how He loved him!” and the "him" is Lazarus. The Jews are pointing to His love for the man who died. Their words don't mention the sisters.

explanations.answer: See how tired He is from the road
explanations.explanation: The Jews don't say anything about the road or being tired. They say, “See how He loved him!” Their eyes are on His tears and what they show. The text gives us love, not tiredness.

True. Some of them asked, “Could not this man who opened the eyes of the blind also have kept Lazarus from dying?” That's in John 11:37. The text says "…some of them…" and it comes right after others said, “See how He loved him!”

The text says they did. Some of them asked, “Could not this man who opened the eyes of the blind also have kept Lazarus from dying?” That's in John 11:37. It comes right after the Jews said, “See how He loved him!”
Cave it is. John 11:38 says the tomb was a cave with a stone laid across the entrance. That stone is going to matter in a minute, friend. Keep your eye on it.
The text doesn't call it a pit. It says the tomb was a cave with a stone laid across the entrance. A pit goes down, while this has an entrance with a stone across it. So the word is cave.
A trench isn't what the text says. Lazarus's tomb was a cave with a stone laid across the entrance. That stone is going to matter in a minute. The word John uses is cave.
Yes, and she doesn't dress it up. Martha, the sister of the dead man, says, “Lord, by now he stinks…” and then, “It has already been four days.” That's a woman who tells it straight.

Martha doesn't say anything about the weight of the stone. What she says is, “Lord, by now he stinks…” Then she adds that it has already been four days. Her words are about the four days, not the stone.

The text doesn't have Martha say that. Her words are, “Lord, by now he stinks…” and then she says it has already been four days. She's the dead man's sister, and she's talking about him. The crowd isn't part of her answer.

explanations.answer: If she believed she would see the glory of God
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says, “Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?” He's reminding her of something He already said. Then they take the stone away.

explanations.answer: If she prayed she would find peace again
explanations.explanation: That's not what He says. The text has Jesus say, “Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?” It's about believing and seeing God's glory. Peace isn't part of it.

explanations.answer: If she waited her sorrow would pass
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't say anything about sorrow passing. His words are, “Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?” What He promised is seeing God's glory. The waiting isn't in it.

explanations.answer: So the people will believe the Father sent Him
explanations.explanation: Yes. Jesus says, “…but I say this for the benefit of the people standing here, so they may believe that You sent Me.” He already knew the Father always hears Him. The prayer out loud was for the people standing there.

explanations.answer: So the disciples will learn how to pray
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. Jesus says He prays out loud for the benefit of the people standing there, “…so they may believe that You sent Me.” That's the reason He gives. Learning to pray isn't mentioned.

explanations.answer: So Martha will stop being afraid
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give that reason. Jesus says it's for the benefit of the people standing there, “…so they may believe that You sent Me.” It's about believing that the Father sent Him. Fear isn't mentioned.
Yes! Jesus called out in a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!” It's three words, said loud. And the man who had been dead came out.
Jesus doesn't say that. His words at the tomb are, “Lazarus, come out!” He's telling Lazarus to come out. The text has a loud voice and a clear command.
That's not in the text. What Jesus calls out in a loud voice is, “Lazarus, come out!” It's a command to Lazarus, nothing more. He doesn't say anything about the sisters when He calls.

Not what the text says. The man who had been dead came out with his hands and feet bound in strips of linen. His face was wrapped in a cloth too. So something was binding his hands and feet, and that makes the statement false.
Right, false. Lazarus came out with his hands and feet bound in strips of linen, and his face wrapped in a cloth. He was still all wrapped up. That's why Jesus tells the people there what to do next.
Yes. Jesus told them, “Unwrap him and let him go…” Notice who He's talking to: the people standing there. They get a job to do after the miracle.
Jesus doesn't say bless. His words are, “Unwrap him and let him go…” Lazarus is still wrapped in strips of linen and a cloth. So the first job for the people standing there is to take it off.
That's not the word. Jesus says, “Unwrap him and let him go…” The man who had been dead came out wrapped in linen. The instruction is about taking off the wrappings.
